stories.headline: J.J. McCarthy wowing Giants after initial concerns over QB's 'maturity,' VP says
stories.summary: Chris Mara said the Giants were concerned by J.J. McCarthy's maturity before the 2024 draft but says the QB has impressed his new team "on and off the field."
stories.body:
The New York Giants seriously considered drafting J.J. McCarthy out of college because they were wowed by his physical skills.

But McCarthy's development off the field over the past two-plus years also has impressed Giants brass, according to Chris Mara.

In a wide-ranging interview with the New York Post, Mara -- the brother of Giants owner John Mara and the team's senior vice president of player personnel -- discussed McCarthy's growth since being drafted by the Minnesota Vikings.

"We had him rated very high from a skill set. ... We weren't quite sure about the maturity level, but we loved his skill set," Mara told the Post, which published the interview Saturday. "He showed the ability to win, the ability to lead."

The Giants acquired McCarthy earlier this year in a trade with the Vikings, who used the 10th pick on the former Michigan star in 2024.

"Seeing him three years later, this is a completely different-looking person for me," Mara said.

The Giants debated using the No. 6 pick in 2024 on McCarthy before ultimately selecting wide receiver Malik Nabers. New York landed McCarthy less than three years later, sending a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Vikings in the Sept. 28 trade.

After missing his entire rookie season because of a knee injury, McCarthy struggled with the Vikings last year, completing 57.6% of his passes with 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions. He lost his starting job with the Vikings in training camp to Kyler Murray and was demoted to third string after an ankle injury kept him out of Minnesota's preseason finale.

But McCarthy has enjoyed success during his brief stint in New York, leading the Giants to an overtime upset victory against the Texans in Houston two weeks ago.

"I'm in awe when I watch him in practice," Mara said. "He's got a much better arm than I thought he ever had. He moves around great. Listen, the arrow's up on him too."

Mara reiterated that since joining the Giants, McCarthy has shown signs of maturity, which was an issue during his time with the Vikings.

"On the field and off the field [he looks different]," Mara said. "He's a terrific guy. He's matured. He's married now, has a kid."

McCarthy will make his second start for the Giants against the division rival Eagles in Philadelphia on Sunday.

stories.headline: Bayern Munich's Manuel Neuer set for spell on sidelines with foot injury
stories.summary: Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.
stories.body:
Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer sustained a partial ligament tear in his right foot and will be out of action for "the time being," the club said in a statement on Sunday.

Neuer had to go off with the injury shortly before halftime in Bayern's 2-1 Bundesliga win at Mainz on Saturday.

Bayern's statement did not give a specific length of layoff for the German goalkeeper, only stating it would be 'for the time being'.

"Manuel Neuer will be out of action for FC Bayern for the time being," the club said.

"The captain sustained a partial tendor tear in his right foot during the German record champions' 2-1 win against 1.FSV Mainz 05 on Saturday, as confirmed by an examination by the FC Bayern medical unit.

"Neuer was substitued shortly before half-time at Mainz."

Replacement goalkeeper Jonas Urbig filled in, as he has often done for the veteran Neuer this season. Urbig is viewed as Neuer's long-term successor at the club and the injury presents a chance to demonstrate he can eventually take the role.

The injury is another blow to Bayern's season following Vincent Kompany's battles with issues that saw him collapse at training. He was hospitalised and treated for meningeal irritation, which is an inflammation of the tissue around the brain or spinal cord.

Neuer has only made five league appearances this season, while the 23-year-old Urbig has also made five, including his substitute appearance Saturday.

It was a bittersweet moment for Neuer as he also became Bayern's oldest Bundesliga player at 40 years and 225 days old in the game.

stories.headline: Conor McGregor insists it has to be Max Holloway for final UFC fight
stories.summary: Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.
stories.body:
Conor McGregor has again insisted he only wants Max Holloway for his final UFC fight.

Back in July, Holloway (28-9) defeated McGregor (22-7) via TKO in just 69 seconds, after McGregor injured his right knee in the opening seconds of their welterweight bout in Las Vegas.

Speaking at the BKFC Glasgow post-fight news conference on Saturday, McGregor, 38, once again reiterated his desire to run it back with Holloway.

"It has to be Holloway," McGregor said at the BKFC Glasgow post-fight press conference.

"Just do the f------ thing again. Just do the thing again. The guy didn't engage once. He's the one that called for the stoppage in the fight. He said 'ref, ref!'

"He's the one stopping the fight. Imagine I just said 'yay!' and jumped the fence. I won! He doesn't want to f------ fight.

"On the one leg, he wasn't coming near me. It's so shocking and so heartbreaking to me and I'm still f------ dealing with it. It has to be Holloway. Just f------ dust it off, re-do it."

On the rehab, McGregor stated he's looking for a return potentially before the summer next year and also hinted if Holloway isn't available he could look elsewhere for an opponent.

"I'm on my way back," McGregor said.

"What's it now November? Three months I'm off of surgery. I done this injury before and returned within nine months. So nine months is pre-summer. I just want to go again and again."

"Something might happen, I don't know. But a fighter that fights me, put some respect on my name. If you're not a world champion fighter, if you've not got world accolades to your name, don't utter my f------ name."

The fight against Holloway at UFC 329 was McGregor's first appearance since July 2021 and he has now suffered serious lower-body injuries in each of past two fights, including a fractured leg against Dustin Poirier in 2021.

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: What to know about Sunday's six-pack of showdowns
stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel, broadcast information, stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
As the first full week of November comes to a close, the NHL has a six-pack of games available for fans Sunday.

It's another mixed bag of matchups -- and five out of 12 teams just played Saturday, so conditioning could be a factor.

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Florida Panthers at Boston Bruins

1 p.m. ET (NHL Network) | BOS -135, O/U: 6.5

Since these two teams have both been good for the past handful of seasons, any matchup between them has had explosive potential. That's especially true after former Bruins captain Brad Marchand began skating for the Panthers after a midseason trade in 2025.

Sadly, Marchand is unlikely to play in this game given he is still recovering from a knee injury. But he is with the team on this road trip, so perhaps fans will get to see him on the jumbotron at some point.

In terms of the players who will be hitting the ice, Matthew Tkachuk (25 points in 17 games) and David Pastrnak (22 in 17) lead Florida and Boston, respectively, in scoring.

Florida enters this game five points back of the first-place Bruins. What will be the gap after the game is over?

Vegas Golden Knights at Buffalo Sabres

3:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | BUF -108, O/U: 6.5

Every time the Golden Knights play in Buffalo, it's a chance for Sabres fans to let Jack Eichel know how they feel about him following the trade that sent him to Vegas in 2021. And the good news is that this particular Sunday afternoon tilt does not conflict with a Buffalo Bills game; they're on "Monday Night Football" this week!

Both of these teams made the playoffs in 2026, but Vegas has looked more like a 2027 playoff team than Buffalo thus far. The Sabres are 3-4-0 in home games this season, and they'd obviously love to get that record well above .500.

Eichel paces the Golden Knights in scoring (23 points in 18 games), while the Sabres are led by his U.S. Olympic teammate Tage Thompson, who has 19 points through 16 games.

Tampa Bay Lightning at Winnipeg Jets

6 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TB -125, O/U: 6.5

Regular readers of NHL Tonight will be aware that the Lightning had a big game Saturday against the Minnesota Wild. What will they have left for the Jets a day later?

These two clubs met on Oct. 29, resulting in a 6-4 win by the Lightning. Tampa built a 5-1 lead after two periods, then Pontus Holmberg netted the empty-net dagger after Winnipeg had scored three straight to pull within one.

It's not often that teams finish with 10 combined goals in a game, but sign us up for another one like that!

New Jersey Devils at Toronto Maple Leafs

7 p.m. ET (NHL Network) | NJ -135, O/U: 6.5

Both the Devils and Leafs watched the 2026 playoffs from home, but both appear destined to be in the mix for berths this spring. If the season ended today, the Devils would have the Metro's No. 2 seed, while the Leafs would be two points back of the Panthers for the second Eastern wild card.

Toronto enters this one a bit banged up, with Kirill Marchenko, Miles Wood and Nick Blankenburg (among others) on the injury report; Seamus Casey is all alone on New Jersey's.

The Devils have gone 6-1-0 since their trade to land Connor Hellebuyck, including four wins in his starts. The Leafs made their big goaltender acquisition in the summer, signing Sergei Bobrovsky in free agency; unfortunately, he has sputtered a bit out of the gate, going 3-7-2 with a 3.34 goals-against average and .886 save percentage.

Up front, Toronto's Auston Matthews is having a bounce-back campaign and sits among the top 10 in scoring with 27 points through 18 games. Fellow USA Olympian Jack Hughes is a bit off that pace with 23 points through 17 games, and scored the OT game winner for New Jersey against the Islanders on Saturday.

Philadelphia Flyers at Calgary Flames

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | PHI -118, O/U: 6.5

On Jan. 31, 2025, these two teams made a trade in which forwards Morgan Frost and Joel Farabee headed to Calgary, with Andrei Kuzmenko, Jakob Pelletier and two draft picks heading to Philly.

In hindsight the deal looks quite lopsided. Farabee (16 points in 17 games) and Frost (12 in 17) are among the Flames' leading scorers, while Kuzmenko is now in Pittsburgh and Pelletier is in Tampa. One of the picks was used on Michigan State's Shane Vansaghi -- so maybe he can become the key piece back for Philly at some point.

In terms of this season alone, expectations have not been met for the Flyers (with a 4-10-4 record after making the 2026 playoffs), while the Flames have been a fun watch as they perform better than predicted. Matvei Michkov has been a bright spot for Philly, as he's scored 10 goals in 18 games after scoring 20 in 81 in 2025-26.

Pittsburgh Penguins at Anaheim Ducks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | ANA -135, O/U: 6.5

Following a 5-2 win over the Kings on Saturday, the Penguins head to Orange County for a matchup against their avian adversaries.

A five-game losing streak in the middle of October looked ominous for Anaheim, but they've since straightened things out and have won four straight. A critical part of the win streak has been their scoring habits, with five or more tallies in each W.

The Penguins had their own four-game losing streak in the middle of October, but haven't really pulled out of the tailspin since; following two W's, they'd lost four in a row again prior to the W against the Kings. Can this be the start of something special?

Reminder: Fans can catch all the action in the NHL streaming hub and on the ESPN App.

stories.headline: Making sense of Jaylen Brown's previous impact with Celtics
stories.summary: Ahead of the 76ers-Celtics game, we dive into the gap between Brown and on/off statistics.
stories.body:
If the Dallas Mavericks' infamous trade of Luka Doncic produced waves of shock and outrage across the NBA, then the Boston Celtics' trade of Jaylen Brown a year later was met with considerably more complicated reactions. Outrage, yes, from Celtics fans -- but also a fierce debate about Brown's on-court value and broader questions about how to analyze players in the modern, data-infused NBA.

Brown is a five-time All-Star, a former Finals MVP and the sixth-place finisher in regular-season MVP voting in 2026, after he averaged a career-best 28.7 points per game. Yet, advanced stats were more skeptical of his stardom. The Celtics had a better net rating with Brown off the court than on it in seven of his 10 seasons in Boston, including each of the last four. (All on/off data in this piece comes from Cleaning the Glass, which strips out garbage time.)

With Brown poised to play against his old team for the first time on Tuesday (8 p.m. ET, NBC/Peacock) -- and with the NBA's best current rivalry poised to begin a new chapter -- it's the perfect time for a deeper dive into what exactly the gap between Brown's reputation and advanced stats means, and how it contributed to the summer's blockbuster trade.

Given the statistics explosion in the NBA's ongoing information era, it's easy to access on/off numbers for every player in the league. Based on conversations with both public and team-side analysts, here's the best way to understand how to interpret them.

Jump to topic:

The on/off basics

Interpreting the use of on/off

How on/off contributed to Brown's trade

The on/off basics
A modern NBA front office is inundated with data about every player in the league. Points, rebounds, assists, shot quality, pick-and-roll frequency, isolation efficiency, jump shot release point, maximum footspeed, average body orientation on closeouts, and on and on and on.

The list of individual data points is nearly endless, but in theory, they all serve the same goal: A front office should identify players who can help the team outscore its opponents, rather than players who collect strong statistics in a vacuum.

Often, the players with the best individual stats also provide the most winning impact -- but not always. And those occasional mismatches can yield different and sometimes counterintuitive evaluations of players.

Consider the highly drafted duo in Orlando's frontcourt. Former No. 1 pick Paolo Banchero has more career points, rebounds and assists per game than teammate Franz Wagner. But Banchero has a negative or neutral on/off split in every season of his career -- meaning the Magic have always been better with him off the floor -- whereas Wagner has finished with a strongly positive on/off split every season.

Most of that gap comes on defense: The Magic's defensive rating has been 3.8 points higher with Banchero on the floor across his tenure, while it has been 5.4 points lower with Wagner on the court. Wagner doesn't generate many steals or blocks, but the idea behind on/off data is that he's clearly doing something right on that end, even if it doesn't show up in the box score.

Ask folks around the league about the profile of a player who's more valuable than his basic stats suggest, and they'll often talk about defensive standouts. That group includes players such as Alex Caruso and OG Anunoby, who have played major roles for the past two champions. They've followed in the footsteps of Shane Battier, famously dubbed the "No-Stats All-Star" in a 2009 piece by author Michael Lewis.

It's no surprise that those role players posted exemplary on/off numbers throughout their careers. But that reputation can take a very long time to stabilize. An analyst for an Eastern Conference team said that 10,000 possessions, or about two seasons of data for a starter, is the minimum sample size before on/off data starts becoming useful.

That caution runs counter to the incessant need for information and analysis, even when the new season's samples are unsuitably tiny in early November. For instance, it's tempting to look at Amen Thompson's early on/off data point for the 2026-27 season and think there's something wrong with his development: The Rockets have been a whopping 47.3 points per 100 possessions worse with him on the floor through nine games, by far the worst mark for any rotation player in the NBA.

But experts know that's the wrong way to interpret the data, and they haven't come close to downgrading their opinion of Thompson's value yet.

"The public should not have access to on/off this early in the season," the East analyst said. "It should be banned. I think it's a disservice to the discourse."

Transforming on/off data from 'astrology' to analysis
The problem with on/off data in its raw, preliminary form is that it's subject to all sorts of inherent biases, including that sample size issue.

"I call it astrology for NBA professionals," said an executive for a Western Conference team, "because whatever story you want to tell, you can go and [find confirmation]."

For this reason, professional analysts say they don't typically work with on/off data until they've made a host of adjustments.

To transform on/off data from astrology to analysis, they employ an advanced statistical technique called regularized adjusted plus-minus, or RAPM, which adds in various adjustments to refine the raw data. This process "does a much better job of understanding context and isolating the player's actual impact," said Taylor Snarr, a former analyst for the Jazz and creator of the advanced stat estimated plus-minus (EPM).

Depending on the specific model, RAPM controls for factors such as:

The identity of the other nine players on the court (four teammates and five opponents)
Home-court advantage
When teams are in the bonus
The opponent's 3-point and free throw percentages, which aren't affected by individual defenders
The "rubber band effect," which shows that teams play worse when they're ahead by a large margin (like a rubber band snapping back)
Whether a defense is playing in front of its own bench, which can improve performance

The most important is the first bullet point, largely because it can account for situations in which the same players "are playing together frequently and consistently," Snarr said.

Two years ago, for instance, Christian Braun finished with the third-best on/off swing among rotation players -- but Nikola Jokic finished first, and Braun shared the court with Jokic for the vast majority of his minutes. Without properly adjusting for his teammates, it would look as if Braun -- who is still a solid contributor but not in the elite echelon -- was one of the NBA's most valuable players.

For advanced player value models such as EPM, the next step is to incorporate what's called a "box score prior," which means blending box score statistics into the adjusted on/off mix to give credit to the right players. (Some models also incorporate various amounts of advanced tracking data at this point.) In that Nuggets example, Jokic's box score stats are far superior to Braun's, so the model can be more confident that Jokic is the main driver of that extraordinary on/off split.

These adjustments allow for much quicker, more accurate analysis of players because of how they isolate impact. "Instead of taking 10 years for on/off to be convincing, you can reduce it down to maybe two years with RAPM," said Kostya Medvedovsky, creator of the DARKO projection system.

This general process is now fairly routine for NBA model builders. But it can be more of an art than a science, and the trickier question is "how heavily do you prefer the [box score] statistical components versus the on/off components," the Western executive said. "That's where I think there becomes more of a legitimate debate and variance amongst the nerds."

For a player like Jaylen Brown, whose traditional stats far outshine his on/off impact, that debate plays an outsized impact in his evaluation. If a player value model weights box score stats heavily, then it will likely conclude that Brown is an elite player because of his strong scoring and all-around production.

But if a model weights box score stats less and on/off data more, then it won't be as impressed with the former Finals MVP. Brown's on/off impact on Boston's offense was typically mediocre because he had poor efficiency for a high-usage player and he posted too many turnovers to too few assists.

Public RAPM-style metrics generally consider Brown to be a very good player but not an MVP-caliber alpha. That mismatch is just one reason that his trade was so controversial.

How on/off might have contributed to the Brown trade

It's hard to deny that the proliferation of on/off-based metrics in both the public discourse and NBA front offices has transformed the league over the past couple of decades.

"I think what's changed the most is the acceptance among nontechnical people," the Western Conference executive said. "Not because they've sat down and taken in those lessons [from analytics], but just because the way everyone understands players has shifted, I think because of the success of those kinds of metrics in helping teams identify and evaluate talent."

It helps that many of the best-run franchises clearly abide by the principles of adjusted on/off data. Executives point to the Celtics and Thunder as two of the teams best known for "RAPM maxxing," which is observable from the kinds of players those teams tend to acquire. Derrick White, Isaiah Hartenstein and Caruso have always rated well by adjusted on/off metrics.

In fact, Caruso's teams have been better with him on the court in all nine of his NBA campaigns, across three separate organizations and two championships. There's a reason both DARKO and EPM rate Caruso as a top-30 player in the league on a per-possession basis, even though he has never averaged more than 10.1 points per game in a season.

Granted, not every RAPM-influenced move is going to be a slam dunk. Analysts point to the Thunder's acquisitions of Patrick Patterson in 2017 and Gordon Hayward in 2024, who were both RAPM darlings before busting in Oklahoma City. Patterson notably posted double-digit on/off swings in the positive direction in his last two seasons in Toronto, right before posting double-digit on/off swings in the negative direction in his two seasons in Oklahoma City.

But those unsuccessful acquisitions didn't stop the Thunder from continuing to trust their models, rival analysts say. And it's that mindset that led them to add Hartenstein and Caruso in the same summer. The Thunder were champions a year later, with Caruso maintaining his positive on/off streak in each season with Oklahoma City so far.

Another player with positive on/off splits in every season of his career is Paul George, across his stints in Indiana, Oklahoma City, LA and Philadelphia. Just one glance at this graph comparing the yearly on/off splits for George and Brown shows why Boston might have preferred to trade the latter for the former, even before considering financial considerations, draft picks or Brown's behind-the-scenes fit in Boston.

Many league insiders were still taken aback by the Celtics' return for an MVP candidate in his prime when they dealt Brown to Philadelphia for George -- who, despite his impressive on/off track record, is older, injury-prone and highly paid -- and picks over the summer. But it wasn't exactly a secret that Boston wanted to trade Brown, so other interested teams had the opportunity to beat the 76ers' offer if they thought signing the Finals MVP was worth a higher cost.

That no better offer came demonstrates just how deeply the lessons of adjusted on/off metrics have permeated the thinking of most front offices.

"In some ways, the Jaylen Brown case is the purest proof of this," Medvedovsky said. "It seemed like: You're trading a Finals MVP, so you're going to get a ton of value for him. But then we saw you just didn't."

This wasn't a case of one ahead-of-his-time, outside-the-box general manager making a shrewd move; rather, it was a case of 28 other general managers not making an all-in offer for a player with underwhelming adjusted on/off metrics.

Now in Philadelphia, however, Brown is attempting to prove that there should have been a massive market for his services: He's averaging 21.6 points per game while often serving as the third or fourth option on the East-leading, 8-2 76ers.

And while it's far too soon to come to any meaningful conclusions about Philadelphia's performance splits with and without him -- Brown has played just 678 possessions as a Sixer, per Cleaning the Glass, or less than 10% of the way to 10,000 -- one early-season data point is mighty compelling.

With Brown on the floor, the 76ers have outscored their opponents by 4.3 points per 100 possessions; without him, they're at minus-1.9. That 6.2-point swing, if sustained, would represent the second-best single-season on/off of Brown's career.

"With [Daryl] Morey gone," Medvedovsky added, "there's no GM who I would identify as, this is the stats GM. But in some ways, it's like a total victory for the on/off data that even with no visibly stats GM, even the non-stats people were on/off-pilled enough that there just wasn't that kind of massive market for Jaylen Brown."

stories.headline: São Paulo Grand Prix 2026: Race in Brazil start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1 heads to Brazil for the São Paulo Grand Prix, a week after Kimi Antonelli was crowned world champion.
stories.body:
Formula 1 heads to Brazil for the São Paulo Grand Prix, a week after Kimi Antonelli was crowned world champion.

The Mercedes driver finished the Mexico City Grand Prix in third and made history by becoming Formula 1's youngest-ever world champion.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the race, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton behind in second.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 20th round.

- The families that built Kimi Antonelli, F1 world champion

- How Kimi Antonelli overcame George Russell, Ferrari to become F1's youngest champion

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the São Paulo Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Autódromo José Carlos Pace
Situated in a neighbourhood between two artificial lakes, Interlagos (which translates to "between lakes"), first opened as a race track in 1940. Formula 1 first raced at the circuit in 1972 as a non-championship race before becoming part of the calendar from 1973.

It dropped off the calendar in 1980 after its bumpy surface was considered dangerous, but F1 returned to a shortened and updated version of the circuit in 1990, which coincided with the rise of Ayrton Senna to global stardom. Senna's S at Turn 1 is one of the best overtaking spots on the track.

The circuit is one of the drivers and fans favourites. It's short, undulating nature, mixed with changing weather, often produces a blockbuster race.

Most wins: Alain Prost with six at Interlagos & Jacarepagua (1982-1984-1985, 1987-1988, 1990) and Michael Schumacher has four at this circuit (1994-1995, 2000-2002). Other winners from the current grid are Hamilton (2016, 2018, 2021), Verstappen (2019, 2023, 2024), George Russell (2022) and Lando Norris (2025).

Most poles: Ayrton Senna with six (1986, 1988-1991, 1994). Previous pole sitters on the current grid are Fernando Alonso (2005), Hamilton (2012, 2016, 2018), Russell (2022), Verstappen (2019, 2023) and Norris (2024 and 2025).

Weather forecast

The weather for the São Paulo Grand Prix is due to be cloudy during Friday's practice, with thundery showers forecast on Saturday with highs of 27°C. Sunday looks like it will be light showers, with temperatures dropping to 19°C.

What happened last time out?

Norris carried his winning momentum into Brazil and put his McLaren on pole position. The Brit then went on to take a dominant victory in Sunday's race.

He extended the lead in the drivers' championship to 24 points from teammate Piastri with three races of the season remaining.

Verstappen had a remarkable drive after struggling with the car in qualifying. For the race, the Red Bull driver started from the pit lane so the team could fit a new engine and change the car set-up, and ended up recovering to finish third.

Mercedes' Antonelli finished second, with his teammate Russell in fourth.

Who will win this year?

Antonelli clinched his maiden world title last time out, so the pressure will be off his shoulders now after getting the job done in Mexico City. He could also break a few more records including most wins in a maiden championship season.

Verstappen leapfrogged to second in the title standings and won the race last week to take his third victory this season, so could be a threat to Mercedes.

Hamilton sealed his first pole position last time out for Ferrari and looked more comfortable in the car. The seven-time world champion, who is an honorary citizen of Brazil, has always been one to watch at this track.

Despite the drivers' championship being wrapped up, the constructors' is all to play for. Mercedes are in mathematical contention to win it in Brazil and will be looking to maximise points from both Antonelli and Russell.

The team need to outscore Ferrari by three points or more.

stories.headline: LA Galaxy miss playoffs again as Real Salt Lake gets final berth
stories.summary: Sergi Solans and Zach Booth scored early and Real Salt Lake clinched a playoff spot while eliminating the LA Galaxy with a 2-1 Decision Day victory over the Galaxy on Saturday.
stories.body:
Sergi Solans and Zach Booth scored early and Real Salt Lake clinched a playoff spot while eliminating the LA Galaxy with a 2-1 Decision Day victory over the Galaxy on Saturday.

Real Salt Lake (13-15-6) snags the ninth and final postseason berth in the Western Conference and will travel to Seattle for a wild-card matchup with the Sounders. The winner will square off against the top-seeded Vancouver Whitecaps in the best-of-three first round.

The Galaxy (11-12-11) have missed the last two postseasons after winning the World Cup in 2024.

Solans and Booth scored three minutes apart to give Real Salt Lake a 2-0 lead in the 13th minute.

Solans used assists from Noel Caliskan and defender Philip Quinton in the 10th minute to score for the 14th time in his first season in the league. Nine of Caliskan's 11 career assists and all three of Quinton's have come this year.

Booth scored unassisted three minutes later for a 2-0 lead. It was the first goal for the 22-year-old rookie midfielder in his 18th appearance and seventh start.

The Galaxy cut it to 2-1 in the 40th minute thanks to an own goal by Real Salt Lake defender Luc de Fougerolles, making his seventh appearance in the league.

Rafael Cabral totaled one save for Real Salt Lake.

JT Marcinkowski saved six shots for Los Angeles.

The Galaxy beat Real Salt Lake 2-1 at home to close out April.

stories.headline: Witness: Clase 'inside' pitch info dried up amid Mizuhara case fallout
stories.summary: A witness said that the inside info he used to bet on Clase pitches dried up due to increased scrutiny from the scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- A government witness testified Friday in the federal trial of Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz that the inside information he used to bet regularly on Clase pitches in 2023 dried up the next season due to increased scrutiny from the gambling scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter at the time.

Luis de Aza Baez said he placed dozens of bets and won thousands of dollars by wagering on the velocity of select Clase pitches during the 2023 season, "because I had inside information." Clase is accused of conspiring with bettors to rig 18 pitches over three seasons.

De Aza Baez said that when he asked for more information on Clase pitches in 2024, he was told that because of "what was going on with Ohtani, there was no more information like that."

Ohtani, the Los Angeles Dodgers' superstar, came under scrutiny in March 2024 after ESPN reported that millions of dollars had been sent from his bank account to an illegal bookmaking operation. His longtime interpreter, Ippei Mizuhara, later pleaded guilty to stealing nearly $17 million from Ohtani to pay off gambling debts and is currently in prison. Ohtani was cleared of any wrongdoing.

De Aza Baez, who worked as an Uber driver, told prosecutors that he began receiving information about the pitches from Enoc Pena, an associate of Clase's, in 2023. De Aza Baez said the tips often came through a group chat titled "Uber Inc." that Pena started and included other men who have been referenced in the case and also worked for the ride-share company in Massachusetts at the time.

Prosecutors showed a screenshot of a text message Clase allegedly sent to Pena on Sept. 30, 2023, when the Guardians were scheduled to play the Detroit Tigers, that talked about "killing the first two chickens." De Aza Baez said the message was instructions to bet on a Clase pitch to the third batter of an inning, but only if Clase had retired the first two batters. Clase did not appear in the game.

Clase's defense has argued that mentions of roosters and chickens in such communications often were referencing cockfighting, a legal activity in the Dominican Republic, where Clase and others in the case are from.

De Aza Baez said he became friends with Pena as well as Robinson Vásquez Germosen and Luis Arismendy Paca Méndez, who are co-defendants in the case, while they were all living in Nantucket, Massachusetts. Paca Méndez, who has pleaded not guilty, is not participating in the trial after being extradited from the Dominican Republic to the U.S. on Oct. 19.

De Aza Baez said he met Clase when Vásquez and Pena brought the pitcher to his house for a birthday party on April 28, 2023, in Winthrop, Massachusetts, where De Aza Baez had moved. He met Clase again a few days later at a relative's house. Prosecutors showed a video of the gathering, with Clase playing dominoes on a table featuring a Boston Red Sox logo. The Guardians were in town for a series against the Red Sox.

De Aza Baez said he never received any information directly from Clase, only from Pena. De Aza Baez said he did not have an agreement with Pena but gave him money because he "almost always" won using the information to bet on Clase's pitches. De Aza Baez acknowledged opening a DraftKings betting account under his wife's name to increase the amount he could wager and win on his Clase bets. De Aza Baez also said he included the Clase pitch bets in parlays to maximize payouts.

De Aza Baez acknowledged that he had agreed with the government to forfeit $69,000 from his winning bets on Clase and would "tell the truth" in exchange for prosecutors dropping a wire fraud charge related to the case.

Clase, Ortiz and Vásquez have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges of wire and honest services fraud, sports bribery and money laundering.

"Our defense is the same today as it was in opening: This is a case about big talk and small bets," Vásquez's attorney Todd Spodek told ESPN after Friday's hearing. "We're confident leaving that judgment to the jury."

The trial will continue next Thursday in Brooklyn.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: Kangaroos into World Cup final after thrashing Samoa
stories.summary: Australia have thrashed Samoa by 32 points to book a Rugby League World Cup final clash with New Zealand.
stories.body:
A backflipping Reece Walsh has helped put Australia within touching distance of their fourth-straight World Cup crown as the Kangaroos dismantled Samoa 44-12 in their semi-final.

In their most complete performance of the tournament to date, Kevin Walters' outfit put an ill-disciplined Samoan side to the sword, running in eight tries at Sydney's Allianz Stadium on Sunday night.

Led by fullback Walsh, who scored a hat-trick, the Kangaroos rarely looked troubled.

Australia will face New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane in next Sunday's final as they look to extend their stranglehold on the World Cup that stretches back to 2013.

As fluent as Australia were, Samoa were all at sea in one of their most underwhelming showings since their surprise run to the 2022 final.

With a side stacked with NRL talent and a groundswell of support from their diaspora community, Samoa have a realistic hope of breaking international rugby league's glass ceiling in the years to come.

But on Sunday they made nine errors and gave up 12 set restarts or penalties, while prop Spencer Leniu was sin-binned for dissent late in a disastrous first half.

After a lively pre-game siva tau where they came face to face with the Kangaroos, Samoa were first on the board when Stephen Crichton kicked a fourth minute penalty.

But it was all one-way traffic from then on as Australia asserted their dominance, starting when Tom Dearden scythed through some feeble defence off a scrum play to put the home side on the board.

Jacob Preston pinballed his way over from close range before Tom Trbojevic, Walsh and Bradman Best all crossed to push the Kangaroos out to a 26-2 halftime lead.

Walsh - chosen ahead of James Tedesco for the starting No. 1 spot - celebrated his try with a backflip.

But he was left red-faced soon after halftime when he leapt to claim a Samoa bomb, which Crichton scooped up to score.

The Brisbane fullback soon made amends by slaloming his way through the Samoan defence and palming off Brian To'o to add his second.

Izack Tago barged his way over as Samoa showed something of a fightback.

But again, Walsh was the man in the right place at the right time.

The fullback backed up a Cameron Munster break to add his third before having a hand in Australia's final try to winger Jack Bostock.

stories.headline: Bruno Guimaraes vows 'unbelievable' Arsenal will keep up Premier League title pace
stories.summary: Bruno Guimarães saluted "unbelievable" Arsenal after they stretched their lead at the top of the Premier League with a gritty 1-0 win over Hull.
stories.body:
Bruno Guimarães saluted "unbelievable" Arsenal after they stretched their lead at the top of the Premier League with a gritty 1-0 win over Hull.

Martin Odegaard's 72nd-minute strike settled a tight match in favour of the relentless Gunners, who now have 27 points from their 10 games this season after a seventh successive home win on the spin.

"We had a tough game, they made it feel so difficult for us, but it's impressive numbers," said Brazilian midfielder Guimaraes.

"I'm happy for myself, for the team. We'll keep going. We've been unbelievable."

The only blip on Arsenal's record in the league was the 3-0 defeat at Brighton in September.

The Gunners had to stew on that one for three weeks over the last international break, but they will have a spring in their step when they link up with their countries this time around.

"The message for us was clear in the dressing room. The last time we had a break, we lost to Brighton in one of the worst games of our season," added Guimaraes.

"The message here was to leave in a good way and go to our internationals happy."

Guimaraes had an excellent game in the centre alongside first Declan Rice and then Mikel Merino after the England man went off on the hour.

Boss Mikel Arteta believes his £75million summer signing from Newcastle is starting to come into his own in red and white.

"He's much better, he had a massive impact, he's hitting serious levels now, but we can still take him to another level," said Arteta.

"That's my conviction, I told him that in the dressing room. He owned a lot of moments in the game, but there is still much more to come."

Saturday's victory was the 34th time Arsenal have won 1-0 under Arteta in the Premier League.

Last week's 1-0 success at Liverpool was branded a defensive masterclass, but this time Arteta pointed to the chances the Gunners squandered against Hull.

They were through on goal twice but Kai Havertz and Noni Madueke could not convert, while there was also a contentious penalty decision which was not given after Havertz was pulled back by Nobel Mendy.

"We need to be more efficient," admitted Arteta. "We were one-on-one with the keeper twice, and if there was a penalty there too...

"There are shots deflected, blocked. We need to insist, to find ways to be more efficient and pragmatic.

"Sometimes we try to score the perfect goal against low blocks, but we need to be much more chaotic than that. If we open the scoring much earlier also, it changes the game."

stories.headline: Does Man United's coach matter? Could Jurgen Klopp reach Premier League glory at Old Trafford?
stories.summary: If Manchester United hired an all-time great like Jurgen Klopp, would they have won the Premier League? Let's find out!
stories.body:
Right around this time every year, you can start to feel it. The air gets a little crisper. The shadows get a little colder. The days get shorter. The tree colors start to pop. You start wearing sweaters. Pumpkins appear in places where they do and do not belong.

Everyone and everything starts to shift, just slightly, in preparation for what's about to happen. The cycles of nature can be fickle and unpredictable, so the date is never exactly the same, and some years come and go without anything at all. But most years, it does.

Our tiny little rituals prime us to anticipate the inevitable, oncoming shift: that moment when Manchester United fire their manager and convince themselves that the new guy is finally going to be the one who fixes everything.

Ruben Amorim lost his job last January. Erik ten Hag was fired two years ago, right before Halloween. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer got the boot just a couple of days before Thanksgiving. And Jose Mourinho was relieved of his duties a little over a week before Christmas.

Now that we've once again entered the season of sacking, Michael Carrick seems like he will inevitably become the latest victim.

Man United are clear of the relegation zone on goal differential alone. If history is any indication, their comeback against AS Roma in the Champions League will end up being meaningless. Before Tuesday's win, Carrick appeared to be on the verge of tears at the end of every match.

This is the 14th season since Manchester United last won the Premier League. And whoever replaces Carrick will be the ninth coach to try to do something that no other United manager since has done: just, simply, meet the expectations at one of the richest sports teams on the planet for more than a single season in a row.

But given how many different coaches have now failed since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club, it makes you wonder: Could anyone have been successful at Manchester United?

What is a great manager worth?

Arsenal won the Premier League last season with 85 points.

If we lived in a world where there were no subs and everyone on the field contributed exactly evenly to their team's success, then all 11 Arsenal players would have contributed about 8 points (7.7, to be slightly more exact) of value last season.

Except, the alternative to each player isn't just zero points. If you removed Bukayo Saka from the lineup, you wouldn't have to play a man down. No, you'd get to put another player out there who would also contribute to winning to some degree.

So, let's look at the relegation-level cutoff. West Ham were relegated with 39 points. Using the same framework, we'd say that all of their players were worth a little over 3.5 points across the season. We could then say that the average Arsenal player provided 5 more points of value than a relegation-level player.

This, of course, isn't exactly how it works: Some players are better than others, some positions are more valuable than others, and almost nobody plays 100% of the minutes. Goalkeeper David Raya played 97.3% of the league minutes last season, and Declan Rice led all outfield Gunners with 90.5% of minutes played.

But it all still gives us a nice benchmark. The best players on the best teams in the world are probably worth around 7 points more than your average relegation-level player. The truly generational superstars? You could probably bump that number up to 10 points if you wanted to.

But what about the manager? Rather than litigating the whole "managers don't matter" conversation for the 1,000th time on this website, we're just going to go with the logic put forth by Liverpool's former director of research, Ian Graham, in his book, "How to Win the Premier League": "[About] the same value as a good player brings. This is in line with manager salaries -- the best managers are paid a similar wage to the best players."

Who, then, was the best manager that Manchester United could've hired at any point over the past 14 seasons?

Most soccer-watchers would agree that there are two potential answers: Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. And most analyses would agree.

A 2025 study from the Sloan Sports Analytics conference looked at team performances from 2017 through 2024 across Europe's Big Five top leagues. The study awarded or penalized the manager for how much a team's performance level exceeded or undershot expectations based on the talent of the roster. Klopp and Guardiola topped the list -- with a significant gap between themselves and the next tier of coaches.

Given the 114 guilty charges against Manchester City under Guardiola, though, I think we have to go with Klopp. While Guardiola's influence on how the sport is played is undeniable, we now have to look on his Man City tenure skeptically. We know how much they outperformed what we were told they spent, but it would be foolish to blindly accept those numbers and attribute the gap purely to the Guardiola effect.

With Klopp, though, we know that he turned two clubs that were not even the richest clubs in their own leagues into two of the best teams in the world. And we know that he maintained those levels -- at both clubs -- for many seasons in a row. On top of that, both Borussia Dortmund and now Liverpool seem to have gotten worse after he left each job.

The job of the manager, simply, is to make his team better than the talent his club can afford to acquire and then to keep that improvement going even as the roster turns over. At the highest level of the sport, Klopp was better at that than any of his peers.

Could the best manager in the world save Manchester United?

What, then, might've happened if Manchester United somehow managed to hire Jurgen Klopp back in 2013 instead of David Moyes?

There are, of course, all kinds of ripple effects we could tease out -- what it would've done to German soccer, where Liverpool would've ended up, how Mohamed Salah's career would've played out, and on and on.

But I just want to focus on what it would've meant for Manchester United. We know that Liverpool benefitted from hiring Jurgen Klopp. But we also know that Jurgen Klopp benefitted from working for a club that did things like convincing him to sign Mohamed Salah instead of Julian Brandt.

Liverpool's cutting-edge front office didn't turn the club into the best team in the world, and neither did Klopp. No, it was the combo of the two that did it.

We could say similarly about Borussia Dortmund. At the time, Dortmund were one of the leaders in both youth development and identifying young stars. This meant that Klopp got the ideal kinds of talent, energetic youngsters to play his high-pressing style: Robert Lewandowski, Mats Hummels, Marco Reus, and Ilkay Gündogan -- just to name a few.

What we know about Manchester United, broadly, is that the club is an abject disaster. In terms of doing things that increase their chances of winning games, they are pretty much as bad as it gets. Since 2013, United have finished at or higher in the table than their relative Premier League revenue ranking once -- and that was last season.

While we could employ some magical thinking and convince ourselves that the only problem here is that the club can't hire the right coach, that's obviously not true. If it were, it would mean that the club that keeps firing its coaches just so happens to be doing all of the other things right.

No, the failure to find a successful long-term coach is a symptom of all of the other issues that plague the club. They've so badly underperformed their resources for over a decade; we can confidently say there is something deeply wrong with the way Manchester United tries to build its soccer teams.

So, if Klopp were the Man United coach, he wouldn't have fixed all of those problems. No, he would've had to work within that dysfunctional environment. He would've, in other words, ended up with Brandt instead of Salah -- many times over.

But let's sketch out the absolute best-case scenario for this hypothetical. Let's say that United have continued to hire "relegation-quality" managers. And let's say that Klopp's value is equivalent not just to the best player on a title team but to a true, once-in-a-generation superstar.

Neither of those things is true -- United aren't constantly hiring genuinely bad coaches, and Klopp himself would tell you that he's not worth the same as Lionel Messi -- but stretching the effect out to the extreme helps make the point.

Plus, by applying a Messi-like effect every year, we're canceling out some of the other problems with this exercise: not addressing the Manchester City situation, not subtracting points from other teams, not accounting for the increased spending power from an increased performance level, and so on.

If Klopp could've added 10 points to every Manchester United season, here's how things would've changed:

On average, United would've ended up with 76 points per season instead of 66, and their average finishing position would've been 3.8 instead of 5.3.

So, of course: things would be better if Manchester United had employed the best manager of the modern era for the last decade-plus. In this scenario, they would've finished in the top four 10 times, rather than six. Perhaps there would've been a deep Champions League run at a club that reached three finals in four seasons from 2008 to 2011 and hasn't been beyond the quarterfinals since.

But even if we granted Manchester United 13 straight seasons of consistent, transformative, incomparable, once-in-a-generation managerial performance, the team would still find itself right where it sits today: with no Premier League titles since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club.

stories.headline: Kimi Antonelli is F1 champion. But why didn't he get his trophy in Mexico City?
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli is F1 world champion, but he won't get his trophy until December. Why does the sport still deny its champions their crowning moment?
stories.body:
There was one rather significant thing missing from Kimi Antonelli's world championship celebrations in Mexico City: the world championship trophy itself.

Despite becoming the youngest champion in Formula 1 history, the Italian will have to wait until Dec. 12 to get his hands on the prize he has spent his life chasing. That is because, unlike almost every other major sporting competition, F1 does not hand its championship trophy to the winner at the moment of victory. Instead, Antonelli will receive it while wearing a tuxedo, in a sterile hall, at the FIA's annual prize-giving gala dinner in Shanghai in December, six weeks after clinching the title.

It is one of F1's more peculiar traditions, denying the sport the sort of iconic sporting image synonymous with its biggest prizes. Think of the World Cup, the Super Bowl's Vince Lombardi Trophy or NHL's Stanley Cup, just to name three. The moment of triumph and the presentation of the trophy are inseparable. It doesn't have to be a conventional trophy, either. The Masters has turned the previous winner presenting the new winner a green blazer one of the most iconic images in all of sports.

F1's championship trophy, by contrast, seems almost an afterthought. Many fans would struggle to recognise it, which seems crazy for the series which is the pinnacle of motor racing.

It is a shame, too, because it is an impressive piece of silverware. Introduced in 1995, the trophy is made of sterling silver with gold detailing and features the signatures of Formula 1's world champions, stretching back to Giuseppe Farina in 1950.

So why wasn't it visible in Mexico City?

The answer lies in the divide between Formula 1 and its governing body, the FIA.

While F1, owned by Liberty Media, controls the commercial side of the championship, the FIA oversees its sporting and regulatory affairs. The world championship trophy falls under the FIA's jurisdiction -- Antonelli on Sunday officially became the FIA Formula 1 world champion - and its regulations stipulate that it must be presented at the governing body's annual gala.

Liberty Media has been keen to make more of the championship trophy. Sources have told ESPN discussions over a change this year did take place -- as they have for successive years now -- that the trophy be presented to Antonelli the moment he won it this year. However, as has also happened in previous seasons, it was agreed the FIA would stick with the convention of previous seasons and opt against doing anything radically different this time around.

- Antonelli makes F1 history as youngest world champion with maiden title

- Verstappen wins Mexico City GP for Red Bull; Antonelli seals historic title

- Antonelli's historic F1 title: Every record broken and milestone reached

The FIA has long argued that presenting the trophy at its gala is important to the occasion's prestige. The event celebrates champions from across motorsport, including rallying, endurance racing and karting, with the presence of Formula 1's world champion regarded as an important attraction for the younger winners.

There is also a sporting justification, as race results can be challenged or altered after the chequered flag, potentially changing the outcome of a championship. The FIA prefers to wait until those matters are settled before handing over its biggest prize.

That argument has some merit, although less so when Antonelli has wrapped up the championship with four races still to run. It rather falls apart altogether when considering what happens at every grand prix as it is the exact opposite of the practice the FIA puts forward in that instance. Individual race trophies are handed out immediately after the finish, despite those results also being subject to protests, penalties and subsequent disqualifications. If a result changes, the trophies simply change hands.

Look no further than Sunday's race in Mexico City for an example. Antonelli was clutching his third-place Mexico City Grand Prix trophy in his hands at different points during his celebratory moments on the podium and the ceremony which followed. That despite the fact a post-race penalty or protest could have moved him down the order after the fact -- it wouldn't have stopped him being champion, but it would have meant he should not have been on the podium. And yet, he did not have the world championship trophy in his hand for that exact same reason.

There is little reason why the championship should be treated differently to an individual race, especially when the current practice stops the trophy becoming a prize that champions can share with fans in the celebratory moments.

It seems a missed opportunity for a sport which has spent the past decade transforming the way it presents itself to the world. F1 has embraced new audiences, new technology and new ways of celebrating its biggest moments, yet its most prestigious prize remains tied to an awards dinner.

Antonelli will undoubtedly enjoy getting his hands on the trophy in Shanghai. But the moment he became world champion, surrounded by his Mercedes team and thousands of celebrating fans in Mexico City, has already passed and it is a moment Formula 1 cannot recreate.

FRISCO, Texas -- Kaick Ferreira, known simply as "Kaick", scored the go-ahead goal in the 88th and FC Dallas beat Colorado 3-1 on Saturday night to eliminati the Rapids from playoff contention.

Colorado (12-15-7) could have secured a spot in the MLS Cup playoffs with a win.

Dallas (16-8-10) clinched the No. 2 seed in the Western Conference and plays seventh-seeded Portland in the best-of-three first round.

Kaick cut back to evade a defender and blasted a shot from the top of the penalty box under the crossbar and inside the right post that made it 2-1.

Joaquín Valiente put away a first-touch shot, off a cross played by Kaick, that made it 1-1 in the 75th minute and Santiago Moreno capped the scoring in the second minute of stoppage time.

Morgan Whittaker scored a goal for the fourth consecutive game for the Rapids. Nico Hansen had seven saves.

Whittaker, on the counter-attack, put away a first-touch shot off a cross from Georgi Minoungou that gave Colorado a 1-0 lead in the 47th minute. Minoungou, who subbed on to begin the second half, has four assists in the past three games.

Up next Colorado: Season completes.
